lead: An equaliser is a receiver filter that cancels the intersymbol interference left by a non-ideal channel. It stores recent samples on a tapped delay line, multiplies them by adjustable weights and adds them, so that at each symbol instant the wanted symbol appears with little or no spill from its neighbours. The zero-forcing equaliser inverts the channel exactly. The adaptive equaliser learns the weights from a known training sequence and then from its own decisions. These filters appear in DSL, cable modems, Ethernet and mobile receivers.
prereq: You need: 5.1 and 5.2 for the sampled overall response and the zero-ISI target.

sections.h3: The equaliser undoes the channel at sampling instants

blocks.text: A real channel does not deliver a pulse in one symbol slot. A pulse sent at time 0 arrives as a waveform h(t) that leaks across several symbol periods T. At the sampling instants kT the channel is described by its samples hk. The sample at time nT contains the wanted term plus tails from earlier symbols. That spill is intersymbol interference, ISI. Section 5.1 gives the Nyquist condition for zero ISI when the transmitter pulse can be designed freely. A cable or radio channel adds its own hk, so the receiver must repair the damage.

A linear transversal equaliser is a tapped delay line with tap spacing T, weights c<sub>−N</sub> to c<sub>N</sub> and one adder. Its input is the received sample sequence x(n). Its output is y(n) = Σ<sub>k=−N</sub><sup>N</sup> c<sub>k</sub> x(n−k). Here c<sub>k</sub> is the weight on tap k, x(n−k) is the input stored for k symbol periods, and 2N+1 is the number of taps. The equaliser sits after the receive filter and before the threshold device.

The useful measure is the combined sampled response. If h<sub>m</sub> is the channel sample at mT, then v<sub>m</sub> = Σ<sub>k</sub> c<sub>k</sub> h<sub>m−k</sub>. The overall response v<sub>m</sub> is the height at mT of one symbol after channel and equaliser. Zero ISI needs v<sub>0</sub> = 1 and v<sub>m</sub> = 0 for every m ≠ 0. The taps are chosen to make this true as closely as the available taps allow.

The zero-forcing equaliser, also called the inverse filter, sets the weights so that v<sub>0</sub> = 1 and v<sub>m</sub> = 0 for all m ≠ 0. In the frequency domain the channel is H(f) and the equaliser is C(f). The cascade must be flat, so C(f)H(f) = 1 and C(f) = 1/H(f). The zero-forcing equaliser is the inverse of the channel response.

With a finite number of taps the equaliser cannot null every tail. A common choice uses 2N+1 taps and solves 2N+1 linear equations: Σ<sub>k=−N</sub><sup>N</sup> c<sub>k</sub> h<sub>m−k</sub> = 1 for m = 0, and 0 for m = ±1, …, ±N. In matrix form H c = δ. Here c is the column vector of tap weights, H is the matrix built from the channel samples h<sub>m</sub>, and δ is a column vector with 1 in the centre and 0 elsewhere. Solve c = H<sup>−1</sup> δ by matrix inversion. An iterative zero-forcing algorithm does the same job without inversion: it adjusts one tap at a time to null one postcursor, then repeats.

The price is noise enhancement. Where |H(f)| is small, |C(f)| = 1/|H(f)| is large, so noise at those frequencies is amplified along with the signal. At a spectral null, H(f) = 0 and the zero-forcing filter would need infinite gain, so it cannot be built. The minimum mean-square error equaliser is the standard cure: it minimises the combined power of ISI and noise instead of forcing ISI to zero.

sections.h3: Adaptive equaliser: learn weights with LMS

blocks.text: A fixed zero-forcing filter needs the channel response H(f). In a telephone line, a radio link or a cable modem the channel is unknown at start-up and drifts with temperature and ageing. An adaptive equaliser starts with arbitrary weights and updates them from the received data. The usual rule is the least mean square, LMS, algorithm: c<sub>k</sub>(n+1) = c<sub>k</sub>(n) + μ e(n) x(n−k).

Here c<sub>k</sub>(n) is the weight on tap k at iteration n, μ is the step size (a small positive number), e(n) is the error, x(n−k) is the stored input sample on that tap, and c<sub>k</sub>(n+1) is the new weight. The error is e(n) = d(n) − y(n). Here y(n) = Σ<sub>k</sub> c<sub>k</sub> x(n−k) is the equaliser output sample at the decision instant, before the threshold. In training mode d(n) is the known training symbol. In decision-directed mode d(n) = â(n), the slicer output, so e(n) = â(n) − y(n). The update moves each weight in the direction that reduces the squared error.

Training mode sends a known preamble. The receiver knows d(n), computes the error and adapts. After the preamble, decision-directed mode uses the receiver's own decision as d(n). This works when decisions are mostly right; a burst of errors can push the weights the wrong way. The step size is a trade-off. A large μ converges in fewer symbols but the weights jitter around the optimum. A small μ gives a steady setting but takes longer to converge.

figure.caption: The received samples go down a T-spaced delay line, are weighted, summed and sliced. The feedback path is the LMS update that changes the weights from the error.

spec.title: Adaptive linear equaliser
spec.aria: The received samples pass down a delay line, are weighted and summed to a decision, and the resulting error is fed back with the LMS rule to change the weights.

examples.question: A channel has sampled response h<sub>0</sub> = 1, h<sub>1</sub> = 0.5, h<sub>2</sub> = 0.25 and h<sub>m</sub> = 0 for all other m. Design a two-tap zero-forcing equaliser with weights c<sub>0</sub> and c<sub>1</sub>. Find the overall sampled response v<sub>m</sub> for m = 0, 1, 2, 3 and state the residual ISI.
steps: For a two-tap equaliser y(n) = c<sub>0</sub>x(n) + c<sub>1</sub>x(n−1), where the second tap is delayed by one symbol period T. The overall response is v<sub>m</sub> = c<sub>0</sub>h<sub>m</sub> + c<sub>1</sub>h<sub>m−1</sub>, with h<sub>m</sub> = 0 outside m = 0, 1, 2.
Set v<sub>0</sub> = 1. v<sub>0</sub> = c<sub>0</sub>h<sub>0</sub> = c<sub>0</sub> × 1 = c<sub>0</sub>, so c<sub>0</sub> = 1.
Set v<sub>1</sub> = 0. v<sub>1</sub> = c<sub>0</sub>h<sub>1</sub> + c<sub>1</sub>h<sub>0</sub> = 1 × 0.5 + c<sub>1</sub> × 1 = 0.5 + c<sub>1</sub>, so c<sub>1</sub> = −0.5.
For m > 3 all terms are zero because h<sub>m</sub> = 0. The only non-zero unwanted sample is v<sub>3</sub> = −0.125, so the residual ISI is −0.125.
examples.answer: The two-tap zero-forcing equaliser is c<sub>0</sub> = 1 and c<sub>1</sub> = −0.5. The overall response is v<sub>0</sub> = 1, v<sub>1</sub> = 0, v<sub>2</sub> = 0 and v<sub>3</sub> = −0.125, leaving a residual ISI of −0.125 at 3T.
examples.check:
h0 = 1.0
h1 = 0.5
h2 = 0.25
c0 = 1.0 / h0
c1 = -h1 / (h0 * h0)
v0 = c0 * h0
v1 = c0 * h1 + c1 * h0
v2 = c0 * h2 + c1 * h1
v3 = c1 * h2
print(c0)
print(c1)
print(v0)
print(v1)
print(v2)
print(v3)

traps: Zero-forcing cancels ISI, not noise. Near a null in |H(f)| its gain is huge, so the noise at the decision point grows. It is not the low-SNR optimum.

Do not mix h<sub>k</sub> and c<sub>k</sub>. h<sub>k</sub> is the channel sample; c<sub>k</sub> is the equaliser tap. The combined response is the convolution v<sub>m</sub> = Σ c<sub>k</sub>h<sub>m−k</sub>.

In LMS the error is d(n) − y(n), not y(n) − d(n), where y(n) is the equaliser output before the slicer. In decision-directed mode d(n) = â(n), so e(n) = â(n) − y(n). A sign flip makes the weights move away from the optimum and the filter diverges.
More taps do not automatically mean a better zero-forcing receiver. More taps can null more ISI but also raise the noise gain and need a larger matrix inversion.

quiz.q: Write the frequency-domain condition for a zero-forcing equaliser.
quiz.a: C(f)H(f) = 1, so C(f) = 1/H(f), where H(f) is the channel response and C(f) is the equaliser response.

quiz.q: Why does a zero-forcing equaliser amplify noise near a spectral null?
quiz.a: There |H(f)| is small, so |C(f)| = 1/|H(f)| is large. The equaliser applies large gain and boosts noise with the signal. At H(f) = 0 infinite gain is needed.

quiz.q: A channel has h<sub>0</sub> = 1, h<sub>1</sub> = 0.4, h<sub>2</sub> = 0 and zero elsewhere. Find a two-tap zero-forcing equaliser and the overall response at m = 0, 1, 2.
quiz.a: c<sub>0</sub> = 1/h<sub>0</sub> = 1; c<sub>1</sub> = −h<sub>1</sub>/h<sub>0</sub><sup>2</sup> = −0.4. v<sub>0</sub> = 1; v<sub>1</sub> = 0; v<sub>2</sub> = c<sub>0</sub>h<sub>2</sub> + c<sub>1</sub>h<sub>1</sub> = 0 − 0.16 = −0.16.

quiz.q: In decision-directed mode, why can a short burst of decision errors make an adaptive equaliser fail to recover?
quiz.a: The receiver uses its own wrong decisions as d(n), so e(n) is wrong. LMS updates the weights in a wrong direction, possibly increasing ISI and causing more errors. This is error propagation.

quiz.q: An LMS tap has c<sub>k</sub>(n) = 0.3, μ = 0.01, e(n) = 0.2 and x(n−k) = 0.5. Find c<sub>k</sub>(n+1).
Why is the minimum mean-square error equaliser preferred to zero-forcing at low signal-to-noise ratio?
quiz.a: MMSE balances residual ISI against noise. Zero-forcing forces ISI to zero and may amplify noise enormously. At low SNR the noise penalty of zero-forcing dominates, so MMSE gives lower total error.

quiz.q: What are training mode and decision-directed mode in an adaptive equaliser?
quiz.a: Training mode uses known symbols d(n). Decision-directed mode uses detected symbols â(n) as d(n).

beyond: Not for the exam. In industry, adaptive equalisers appear in DSL modems, cable modems, gigabit Ethernet, disk read channels and wireless baseband chips; many use LMS or its normalised and block variants. Research goes further with decision-feedback equalisers, blind equalisation, fractionally spaced equalisers and maximum-likelihood sequence detection. Newer curricula connect the same LMS rule to neural-network training, where it is called stochastic gradient descent. Search next for "least mean squares adaptive equaliser", "zero-forcing noise enhancement" and "minimum mean-square error equaliser".
